John E. Wood is my name, and I live in Harrisonburg, Virginia, and some people think I talk funny.
I see. What is the E for?
Edwin, as in Edwin, King of England.
Look at how long of the Ed's up with that. E-W-I-N. Edwin, that kind of Edwin.
It's working, huh?
Yeah, I believe so. We can move it a little closer to you.
Okay.
What's today's date?
Today is, I believe, June 26, 1986.
All right. So, tell me a little bit about yourself. Where were you born?

I was born in Richmond, Virginia in 1928, and with the exception of the years that I spent in New Orleans as a graduate student in the late 1950s, I've lived in Virginia almost all of my life. I was in the Army for a while, but other than that, I am a lifelong resident of Virginia. I'm on the faculty of James Madison University in the past five summers. This being the fifth, I have come and taught summer school in the History Department at Tulane, from which institution I graduated with an MA and PhD degree that I earned back in the 50s.
Well, where were you in the service, just out of curiosity?

Out of curiosity, I was drafted in 51 and assigned to an Alabama-Mississippi National Guard division that had been called a federal service. I spent a year in South Carolina with them and another year in Indiana, and then I was released and went back home.
Well, did you hear a lot of jazz in those places, like Virginia and Indiana?

No, no, no, Richard. No? No? I didn't hear much jazz in any of those places. I guess before I came here as a graduate student, I had, as a high school student, I had enjoyed listening to a great variety of music. I had particularly enjoyed some black folk blues people, Lead Belly. I had a great collection of Lead Belly records when I was a high school student. And some Josh White records that I played a lot, Blind Lemon Jefferson records. And I had read a book or two. I can't really even tell you. It was a book that was published, I don't know, I guess the late 40s, called Mr. Jelly Roll. Alan Lomax did it. Yes. I read that book before I came down here. So I had this, you know, just a young man's awareness of the music. But when I came down here, you introduced me to it in a more direct way and I came to enjoy it very much. I remember that one of the first brass band street parades that I attended that you told me about, and I think we went together, my wife then and some other Tulane people. And as we had assembled in front of the neighborhood grocery store where the band was sort of coming together and all these people were standing around, you pointed out and then introduced me to the man who was a drummer of this particular band and his name was Paul Barberin. And I was just dumbfounded because I had, you know, that name was one that I had remembered from reading about as having been somebody who had been a New Orleans musician who had played with bands in Chicago in the 20s and so on. And then there he was standing on the street corner in New Orleans in 1955 or something. It was just quite a surprise to me. And so I used, you know, I came to enjoy very much going to hear the brass bands play whenever we had the chance to go and hear them play. And in 55, 6, 7, 8 in there, there were more chances. There were a fair number of chances. I think back on it, maybe there weren't as many as I sort of thought there were then. But it seemed to me that in the summertime where you could go to a parade practically every weekend.
Yeah.
Wasn't that the case? Really?
It always seemed that way. And if there wasn't one on Sunday, there was a funeral during the week.
Yeah.
Or something like that. And then the...

The occasions were all, what seemed to be, the Sunday school parades, and I remember that traditionally or very often, they would assemble at Shakespeare Park and march to the Booker T. Washington Auditorium. And that was, you know, that was not a long distance, but it was a... And, you know, I don't think I could find either one of those places right now. I could have to look on the map to find them. But... And I always thought that was a very nice way to spend a Sunday morning.
Well, they changed the names of places, too. Yeah. There's no more Shakespeare Park.
Oh, there is.
It may be A.L. Davis Park in Ferret in Washington.
Yeah. Remember that the Ferret Street bus, which is a bus we rode back and forth to go downtown, you know, went right by there.
So it was real easy to get to it on the bus.
So it's not called Shakespeare Park anymore. No. Who was A.L. Davis?
He was a councilman.
I see.
Yeah. But back to Paul Barber and about what year would that have been?

That would have been, I would say, I came here in the summer of 55. And I don't think I really... The first parades that we went to were the following summer. We were here just for the last half of the summer and had just barely gotten oriented to the city and the campus and all of that. And it wasn't, I guess it was the summer of 56. It was probably the summer of 56.
Yeah, well, I mean, to me this is interesting because I've never talked to many people about this. How did we get to know each other?

You and I? Yeah. Through just being in this history department at Tulane. I guess in Hogan probably had said something to me sometime about you. And I probably hunted you up and said, listen, you know, I hear you're interested in the music. And I am too. Where do I go to get to hear something? And you were forthcoming and said, well, you know, come to a parade. There's going to be some things. And then I remember very well, you were very regular. You would call up maybe Friday afternoon or something and say, you know, there's going to be a parade, such and such a place. So if there was a funeral, you would tell me. Or I would see you on the campus and you'd tell me. Were you a graduate student in the history department then?
I was a graduate student around 56, yeah.
Yeah. Yeah, that's it.
That would have been it. That would have been how we met.
Yeah.
But to get to know who was interested in jazz then, you know, it wasn't easy.
Yeah. I think that connection has probably came out of Hogan somehow. Yeah, that Hogan.
Probably did.
And I had said something to him about, you know, I'd like to, I was interested, I'd like to hear some music or something.
You don't remember what band Paul Barber was with. I'm curious.

It didn't register with you. It didn't really. My guess is it was either the Eureka or the, it was probably the Eureka. Because I don't think he played with the Young Tuxedo. It was either the Eureka or the Young Tuxedo. He might have played with the Young Tuxedo. I think he substituted them. Anywhere. Yeah.
They had regular members.
Yeah.
In those bands. And membership was an important thing. But there were also substitutes.
Yeah.
Just don't.
But I remember.
You don't remember how those things happened 20, 30 years ago.

No, no. And I don't remember whether that first parade was one that just had one band or whether they had more than one band. That was fairly often. The Sunday school parades would be big enough occasions that they'd have more than one band in them. And it was, I remember that was kind of a, could be a frustrating thing that you'd pick one band that you wanted to hear. And they would play. And then they would stop playing. And then you could hear another band a block or two back. And you think, oh, gee, I want to go hear them. You go running back the sidewalk. But at the time you got back to them, they would stop playing. And the band you just left would start again. You know. It could be frustrating. Did they both play at the same time? They tended to alternate, as I remember.
That's how I remember it, too. Now, it seems to me nowadays when they have two bands, they can be very close to each other, they'll both play at the same time.
Yeah.
And I suppose that's what you call modern music. By tonality.
Yeah.
All those, all those.

Well, I suppose this parade that I went to just last Saturday had two bands. But they were placed so far apart that you couldn't hear one when you were with the other one. Or you could just barely be. Well, actually, you couldn't hear the other big band. And there was another little pickup band that had about four people in it that was in between the two. And you could maybe hear them a little bit. But they were, they were not really much of a band. But the other two, it's always, I always thought it was some kind of indication that it's an organized band when the band members have hats that have an embroidered name across it. Somebody's gone to the effort to get an embroidered band.
I hate to tell you this, but they can take those bands off.
And switch them from one hat to another.
It was the 21st of June, 1986, that parade you're talking about.
Yeah. And it was the revived Tuxedo Band and also something called the Last, no. Chosen Few Band was the other band.
Is that Fat Anthony?
Tuba Fats? That's Tuba Fats, yeah.
Laysen?
Yeah.
Yeah.

And I didn't really get to hear them play because I walked all the way with the Tuxedo group. And when we got up to the end and they were through playing and turned off of Canal Street, I ran back and heard the Laysen Band play just sort of the last half of their last number. And that was about it.
We can restrict this, but what did you think of that? Well, it's still a continuous existence, but of that, you call it revived, I'd call it revised.
Yeah.
Young Tuxedo. What did you think of it as compared with the one that you heard in the 50s?

Well, it's certainly not the same band, you know. Michael White is not John Casimir and what have you. And they didn't really have a big bass horn, a la Wilbert Tillman. They had, I don't know, I don't know technically enough about the music, Richard, but they had, it was a smaller horn that had flatter twirls on it. What is that? I don't know. I don't know.
It could be a tuba.
No, it wasn't a tuba. A tuba is a great big thing. It wraps around.
You're talking about the sousaphone that wraps around you.
Yeah.
It has another kind of brass bass, but they have.
But the one that the present Tuxedo Band has in them is not one that he wraps around. It's a brass bass that he holds in front of. Yeah.
Some of those are pitched all higher, you know, and they don't.

And he was, he played, it was a younger guy who was playing it, and he really wasn't very prominent in the music. But, you know, I enjoyed the music tremendously, and I enjoyed the experience of just seeing the brass band out in the streets. I've always thought that that was the appropriate place for that music with the sun shining and everybody enjoying themselves in the street. And it's a glorious, happy sound. But it is a very different sound. I don't really, again, know enough technically about the music to really define what those differences are. But it, they did things that I don't remember the young Tuxedo doing and vice versa. You know, that they had a, they, the trombones and either was the cornet or the trumpet. I don't know which it is that Greg Stafford plays. What does he play a trumpet?
He plays cornet. Cornet.
They did a real growling sort of bass and slurring bass runs on things that, I don't remember that the Casimir's band, you know, did that kind of stuff.
Well, it's just, it's a different sound and you wouldn't expect it to be a sound.

No, it's a different, you know, it's, actually Greg Stafford who ended up giving me a ride from that, where that parade ended up, back down to the French market where he was late playing his gig at the Cafe Mediterranean. And I got into that because he had seen me before the parade started talking to, to Barry Ratton. And he had overheard some things that, that Ratton was saying to me, I guess was in response to a question I had asked him about the band that I had heard him play with the week before. And, you know, Greg took a little offense at some, not, I don't know that he knew exactly what Ratton was saying, but what he was taking offense at was Ratton as somebody who was not a New Orleanian being authoritative in telling people about what New Orleanian music was really like when he is not himself of the tradition. I was surprised that Greg was as sensitive about that as he seems to be. And so, you know, he was saying, you know, we don't sound like John Casimir's band sounded like, but, you know, we're, it's 30 years later and everything moves and changes. We shouldn't sound like it. We grow, everybody grows. It's not the same world.

But it's the same tradition. That's basically what he was saying. And I have no real argument with that. You don't want it to be just an antique replica of something else. It's got to be something that's his and of the present. But he was very conscious, and he could articulate that concept, I thought, very well.
Well, do you remember the bass drummer with Young Tuxedo that day? Did you talk to him?
No.
I happened to run into him on the street yesterday. And he remembered you being there with your daughter and her friend. He was commenting on the number of second one, I say.
That prayed on the 21st?
Yeah.
My daughter wasn't there then.
Oh, it wasn't you, your daughter. Okay, it was somebody else himself.

Well, one of my reactions to that parade was that they weren't in the second liners. That the only thing that even came close to it was me and this guy, Carl Peter, somebody from Norway. And he and I walked the whole way from where they started to the end, right along with the Young Tuxedo Band. And every once in a while there'd be a little knot of people on the sidewalk that would kind of get with it a little bit and clap as he went by. But there was basically no second line. And I was very much aware of that. And I noticed, and I wondered if that was because they were going down Canal Street as opposed to going through a residential neighborhood where they might have drawn people into the houses. I remember that. I remember that that was one of the things that used to delight me about going to the Bass Brass Band parades in the late 50s was that whenever the band got assembled and whatever the procession was that they were there for, whether it was a Sunday school parade or a large parade or whether they were playing for a funeral and the funeral group, the club or whatever it was called was assembled. And they would start off that just almost instantaneously. The sidewalks would be full of these really young kids, usually teenage guys with tattered umbrellas and just swooping up and down. They had a little kind of gate step that they did. They went up and down and forward. And it was just marvelous. It was a free, open, sort of joyous, kind of spontaneous thing. And that's why that parade two days ago was really pretty flat in that respect. I mean, they were marching along in the procession of automobiles. You know, they had a whole bunch of convertibles in front of them and behind them containing dignitaries of the church. And nobody heard them except those guys riding in the cars and the occasional person on the sidewalk. It was pretty flat in that respect. And again, to me, it indicates that the brass band tradition as it survives now is really pretty fragile as a phenomenon of the life of the city. That it was just sort of grafted onto that parade. And it really is not, you know, as the sort of part of the fabric of the community that it was 30 years ago, I guess it is.
Well, I know exactly what you're talking about in that case. I'd hate to generalize. Maybe there are things going on that we don't know anymore about.
Yeah.
I guess that's always the case. There are things going on that you don't know anymore. But tell me more about the parade itself. You said there were convertibles. Anything else besides convertibles?

Well, there were floats with, you know, groups from, that had big banners that said, we're from this AME church or from another AME church. And there was a big sort of traditional marching band of young people, high school age people. There was a band from here somewhere. I've forgotten what their drum said. Is there something called the Music Academy or something? It was big. It had probably 40 people in it. And they led the parade and played, you know, just traditional march tunes that were not given a jazz arrangement.
Were they fast?

Pretty fast. And then these people riding in cars who were dignitaries at this. And they seemed to be stopping at a church up there on Romaine. I didn't hang around long enough to see if people were going into the church to have some church gathering up there.
On Roman Street?
Yeah. Just off a canal. We had two blocks on the Down River side of the canal.
Downtown Riverside.
Yeah. But, you know, it was a motorized, pretty much a motorized parade except for the musicians. Again, that was the old parades. Nobody rode in cars. Everybody walked.
No Frenchy Drilled Squad. No banners.

No, they had some banners. And they had some, that in this parade on the 21st, there was, I didn't really see them in the parade, but I saw them before the parade. There were some guys on these little three-wheel things that, you know, you see them in other parades that probably do formations like the Shriners do and that kind of stuff.
Little motorcycle-like things.

But I was there to hear the young tuxedo, so I did try to get some idea of what the context, you know, why somebody had, you know, wanted to have a band to play for that parade. And it was this AME Church's pre-bicentennial celebration.
Do you remember the parade on the 22nd of June, 1958?
I mean, did you? I know that I have documentary evidence that I went to a parade that day.
But you don't remember much.

I remember a little bit about it, yeah. That was a parade with the young tuxedo brass band, and it was not a big parade. It was confined to the neighborhood where that church was. Where was it? Hamburg Street. Mm-hmm. And it was, the parade was a preliminary to a church service. And when they got to the church and everybody went in, the band went home, or the band dispersed. I don't know whether they went home or not.
Some musicians have been known to stop off for a drink.
Yeah. You were at that parade.
Yeah.
Whether you remember it or not. Do you remember it?
No.
Okay.
You remember, a lot of things you'd remember much more clearly than me.

Yeah. Well, because you, that's right, you were more jaded to them. I remember at that parade, I was the first, do you remember this? This is the first time that I, maybe it's not the first time I had heard that the band play just a little while to stay here. But it was the first time that I made an effort to find out what it was, that they were playing it. And you were 20 feet up ahead from where I was walking along. And I ran up and asked you, what's the name of that tune that they are playing? And you had to stop and listen and then tell me. And I remember. It was just a little while to stay here. Yeah. And it continues. Yeah, that's a good, good, good. I always enjoyed the bands playing for those church occasions because they nearly always played hymns. And I particularly enjoyed it when they played hymns in those brass band arrangements. So that gave them such a, to my Virginia Protestant ear, such an unusual and joyful sort of rendition. I always really liked it.
What denomination?
Well, I grew up in the Baptist church and I became a Presbyterian and then I became an Episcopalian.
That's quite a bit of change.
Which, but, yeah. I still, you know, I guess I like the music in my rural Virginia Baptist church better than I like it in my Episcopal church where I really am well placed and established.
Rural Virginia? I thought you were from Richmond.

Well, I have a dual background. I have deep roots in Fluvanna County, Virginia. As well as in Richmond. I spent time in both places. I was born in Richmond, but my family, my grandparents on both sides lived in Fluvanna. And I spent all the summers up there and from time to time lived there as my mother drifted back and forth between the city and the country. So, but I, I, I went, I graduated from high school in Richmond, but I, when I was, my boyhood and early teen years I was in Fluvanna as much as I was in Richmond. And so I have those deep rural roots.

So, the more evangelical Protestant type of faith ties in with all those hymns, I guess. I mean, that's what, that's my guess. Yeah. And probably one of the reasons why I like them. Although, I don't remember them specifically, the hymns they were playing. But then, somebody like Paul Crawford, I don't know if you remember him from those days or not.
Not really.
Paul was a, following the bands, even though he's a tromboneist, he'd listen a lot too.
Yeah.
Uh, anyway, uh, his father was a minister and he knew all those hymns.
Yeah.
Maybe he worked in churches playing music or something. Did you ever see any, uh, drunks at, at, uh, parades? Sure.

Uh, there would, there would be drunks at parades. Uh, this one we talked about, uh, over on Hamburg Street. But, uh, I remember there was somebody who was, uh, followed along and got noisy. And, uh, somebody would, you know, get him to go back up on the porch. But pretty soon he'd be back down again yelling. And, uh, he wasn't really disruptive. But I, I, as, I always felt, Dick, whenever, uh, never really got over this. That when we went to those parades, you met, you were a white person going into a black neighborhood. And, uh, you were, in effect, kind of honing in to hear the music that was really there for some other purpose. And I always felt like I was something of, of an intruder. And, uh, I tried to sort of keep a little bit out of the way and not be, you know, a real intruder. Although it was inescapable, you know, that I was, uh, you know, a stranger who was not really a part of the sort of organic functioning of the occasion. But, uh, as, as, as an intruder and an observer, you, I couldn't help but observe that this guy was, uh, he was pretty drunk. But I think I kind of wrote it off. This is a weekend and he's probably celebrating not having to work, uh, whatever. Or, uh, yeah, they were, but on the other hand, you know, even though I was, um, very conscious of being, uh, you know, a stranger and, and an intruder. Although, because we went often enough that, well, I'm sure that we were familiar faces to the musicians. The sponsoring groups didn't really know who we were. And the musicians made us always feel like they were pleased to have us there to hear them play. Uh, and I don't, I've never known, you know, how much of that was a genuine thing or how much of that was just sort of a politeness, uh, on their part. Whether they cared whether you were there or not. I got the impression that they liked having people appreciate their music and that, but, and I would like to think that that was the case. Um, and, but while I felt that sort of strangeness and being an intruder, I never really, uh, was made by anybody to feel unwelcome. I mean, nobody ever said to me, you know, like, white guy, what are you doing here?
Or anything like that.

Yeah. And, uh, I never felt threatened or menaced in any way at all. Uh, in fact, I remember one day, somewhat to my surprise, uh, having gone to, I believe it was a funeral, and they were playing the warm-up number as they did. They would assemble at some place a couple of three blocks away from where the home was, where the body was, or where the funeral home was. And then they would have a warm-up, play a fast number, go around a block a couple of times. Uh, and that would clear the houses if people just come streaming out onto the streets. Then, and we were kind of bouncing along down the sidewalk, uh, kind of timidly into the second line routine. And all of a sudden, at all of a sudden, at all of a sudden, at all of a sudden, somebody had me by the hand and was pulling me along and, uh, sweeping me up with the whole second line thing. Uh-huh. You know, uh, it was, uh, kind of took me by surprise. And somebody I'd never seen before and probably never saw again. But, uh, it was part of the spectacle. And, uh, it was part of the spectacle.
I was in the midst of it.

But that was always a striking and exciting thing is when at a funeral, and I really didn't go to a lot of funerals, maybe three or four, maybe a couple more, but that they would play that, the band and the club that was the deceased had been a member of, they would assemble somewhere a couple of blocks away and then they would have this warm-up fast number and kind of get right and then get over to the home or the funeral parlor and when they finally brought the casket out then they would go to the church where they want to preach over them and they would play the slow, durage numbers. And they would play the same number sometimes in this March, dead March time as opposed to the fast, happy warm-up time and just change the whole mood of the whole occasion. just in an instant. And the marshal, the person who was the member of the club who was leading the parade and who set the tone of it a lot by his own sort of step and demeanor. also could just change the tone of it just by changing the way he held himself and the way he did his steps going down the street. he had control of that. It was rather remarkable. I always thought that the mood of it could be changed and become very sad ensemble. John Casimir, when he would play for those funeral parades, I've seen him on, I perhaps shouldn't say many occasions, but certainly on more than one occasion when he would be playing the slow marches when they were going to the church or from the church to the cemetery, would become so involved in the music that he would have tears just streaming down his cheeks while he was playing his clarinet. And he was not involved in the occasion. He was just, you know, they were there playing for the occasion. But he just, he got himself so caught up in the emotional power of the music that he, the tears are just streaming down his cheeks while he was playing his horn. And I always found that to be very powerful and very moving, that he would do that. Getting close to the end of your tape.

Yeah, I think we are getting close to the end of the tape, so I'll ask you three or four questions now to confuse you. I'll check it. Okay we got John Wood, Reel 2, and today is the 26th of June 1968.
Not 68.
86, huh?
86, yeah.
Yeah, well I'm going back in my memory.
Yeah.
And watching this tape machine and worrying about it. And I shouldn't. You had brought up something which I thought was interesting. Tell me about going to hear Barry writing, where that was.
Well, I went, I guess it was two weeks ago, the band that he put together to play down in the French market on Sunday afternoon.
The 15th of June, I looked it up.

Okay. Mm-hmm. I had not heard him play before. And I don't think I really recognized any musicians that he had playing with him, although a number of them were sort of older people. But I was just, I was very taken with his playing in particular. And, uh, as I was telling him while we were changing the tapes, that he, they played Just A Closer Walk With V. And he started it out playing in the low register in a slow tempo, that I found very powerful and just freighted with all kinds of emotional overtones for me, that, that, uh, he played it, uh, you know, with a lot of intensity and heart. And, uh, I thought it was very moving. I told him that the other day, as a matter of fact, when I saw him.
Did you know he was a strain when you, Australian when you, when you first?
Yeah. When you first? I knew he was an Australian because you had told me before. Yeah.
It didn't, it didn't matter.

You thought that. No. I thought that he had captured the idiom pretty well. Yeah. Uh, the thing that I talked to him about, uh, I saw him. And he was on the sidewalk waiting for that same parade to start on the 21st and I just fell into conversation with him. And, uh, it took me a while in listening to his band to sort of get my ear used to the, that he had a, somebody, uh, I believe his name was Charles, Buddy Charles maybe? Yeah. Uh, playing the guitar. Uh, and it was kind of a beat up old acoustic guitar that he had an electric pickup on. And it, when I first listened to the band, it, it, it seemed pretty loud in the text of the music. Uh, uh, that it was a stronger presence. Uh, uh, it took my ear a while to get used to that. Uh, uh, and I said something to, uh, Barry Ratton about that when I would just stand on the street corner. And he took that as an occasion to sort of comment that it was his perception that in the early bands, really back really, real early ones, early 20th century, that the guitar was a standard thing. Oh, yeah. And that ordinarily when they, when they played inside, that the sound level, the loudness, was not to be louder than the softest instrument playing at its loudest capacity. Uh, uh, uh, that, that, that they, the band would adjust itself to that. And, um, that, uh, since I guess the guitar that they were playing with that day was, could play pretty loud.
Uh, uh, uh, they could play pretty loud.
Uh, it really was, I, but I, I, as, as I listened to it as the afternoon wore on, I got sore. I really kind of liked it, uh, the guitar whanging away.
And you weren't drinking, were you?
No, no, I wasn't. I was just trying to stay cool in the shade.
But I find that I tolerate more things if I drink. Yeah. Yeah. The Young Tuxedo is playing this Sunday.

I know, and I'm not going to be here. I've got to go to Miami to interview somebody about aviation history. And, and, but the, um, the Young Tuxedo is playing down there Sunday, but, uh, Greg Stafford is not playing with them. So, he.
Gonna have Teddy Riley.
He told me about that too. Yeah. But, he'd be playing across the street.

There's. I think we're catching the feeling of, of, uh, the grapevine that goes on. That I'll see somebody who works with refrigerators for Sears, who's a bass drummer. Yeah. And, uh, you'll run into Greg and is that and the other thing.

It's been interesting to come back and to find that there is as much music as there is. Uh, I, I think, uh, there may, may have been more, I'm sure there was more in the fifties than I was really aware of. Uh, I did not enjoy Bourbon Street music much in the fifties, although, as I may have told you before, I used to, to go to the Paddock Lounge and hear the Bill Matthews Band, which I guess, again, was a band whose members change right much from time to time. But, it frequently had him and Albert, always had him in it. And, and then Albert Burbank was with them quite a bit. Yeah. And I, whenever I could afford the time and the money, I enjoyed going down and hearing them play very much. But that's, hearing them was the only experience in the fifties that I really had on a sustained basis that was not the brass bands in the straights. And I always liked to hear the music in the bright sunshine better than hearing it in the smoky nightclub. Yeah.
What about the big dance halls?
I never went to the dance halls, Dick.
And that's because I kept that a secret.

Well, I don't know that you really kept it a secret. You, you occasionally would mention it. Uh, you never really, you know, pressed me to come on and go. Yeah. Uh, I had a lot of reluctance about going into those places, uh, in part because I felt even more an intruder in, in those settings. You knew those people and, you know, I didn't, uh, if I had not had a, my wife, I might have been more venturesome of that going to again. Yeah. But that was, that would really have been pushing for me into, uh, into somebody else's turf where I would have really felt like I was quite a stranger. And, uh.
You would have felt strange about going to white dance halls.

Not to white dance halls as much as black dance halls. I mean, I, I, I, I might have felt strange about going to white dance halls too, because, you know, it, it, it, it was really just not what I was into.

Well, there were a lot of white dance halls here. And that's what they, primarily the dance halls were for whites, were these bands. Yeah. The, uh, blacks were not often hiring. Yeah. Uh, they did hire John Casimir, for example. Yeah. The blacks would. But, uh, as a rule, they didn't hire old time jazz musicians. Yeah. In those times. Except at, at parades. Yeah. You know, there was a perfect split with some people. They, they would march along and follow the parades and tell you that they didn't like that old time music. But it wouldn't march in the hot sun for hours listening to it. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, I would march for hours in the hot sun listening to it and I was happy to tell you that I loved it.
Yeah. I didn't make any bones about. Yeah.

Turning my nose up at it. There was something that I did want to make sure I told you about and I don't remember whether I told you about this, recall this for you or not. But again, it's within this whole idea that the parades then were, uh, part of the life of the community. Yes. And there was an, an episode that I found just really interesting and also again moving, uh, there was a large parade and again, I don't know, I don't remember where they started or where they went to, but the band played for this group of men who were wearing their large regalia and the band, uh, you know, were, were dressed. I never saw a band that was really had fancy uniforms. They always just had black pants and a white shirt and a cap and stuff. But they, they, they, they marched down the street into the neighborhood and wherever it was that they were going, they were playing and everybody was enjoying playing. And all of a sudden they, they, they, uh, headed down this little narrow side street and, uh, couple of blocks and made a few turns and stopped in front of a modest little shotgun house, uh, and stood outside. And while some of the dignitaries of the large group went to the door and, and, and, and the people in the house came out and stood on the porch and brought out from inside the house and old man in a wheelchair. Mm-hmm. They rolled him out and sat him on the wheelchair on the front porch. And, you know, the band played a couple of numbers, serenaded him and, uh, he was old and frail, but obviously just loved the fact that, uh, he was being honored in that way. And his family felt honored and, uh, large, uh, people felt good that they had come and done that. And the musicians seemed to enjoy it too. And I was practically in tears standing on the sidewalk watching it all. But it was a very, uh, moving kind of thing that they did.
I've been involved in things like that. I agree.

Oh, yeah. And then, you know, they went back up to their regular parade route and went on down the street and ended up at the, uh, Lodge Hall where they were going to have some kind of meeting or party or what have you. And I don't believe, sometimes a band got to go in and have some refreshments and sometimes they didn't. And I believe on that day the band wasn't invited to come in and partake of the food and drink that the group was going to have.
Did you ever get invited in? And this is a good point to ask you about. No, I didn't. Uh, well, you saw.

And I don't think I would have gone, you know, I, don't know. If I had been invited, it would have been an insult not to accept the invitation. But I would have been pretty uneasy about it had I, you know, been in that situation. I guess I'm just as glad I didn't get invited.
Well, yeah. If, if, if they had a rest stop in somebody's yard where a beer was served, you wouldn't have gone into that.
Oh, probably. Yeah. That's kind of fun.
That sort of thing.

And I used to, uh, when they were going to funerals, uh, when the procession would get in the church and they would have that part of it, the preaching and the singing of the choir. Yeah. The band would frequently just be sitting around outside waiting for them to come out. Mm-hmm. And, uh, you know, would sit on a curb and buy a beer at the grocery store on the block down the street and sit and drink a beer with them and talk to the musicians. Uh, or maybe go up and sit on the ground under the church window and try to listen to the choir singing inside. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
But they could stay in there a long time preaching over the deceased an hour sometime.
Oh, sure.
So you had a little time to kill, and it was a hot sunset. So you found a bit of shade, buy a beer, and fraternize with your musicians. On a very casual level. Yeah, oh, yeah.
Not going into the church. Oh, no. You never had to make a statement or testify to the congregation? No. Or going to any of the dinners or anything like that?
Always sort of hanging around in the background.
Yeah, well, you didn't want to intrude.
And actually, that feeling of not wanting to intrude, I never went, I never followed a funeral all the way into the cemetery.
Yeah.
I never went and saw them actually bury the deceased and, you know, just hung around and gawked at that part of it.
Well, it was nobody you knew.
Yeah, well.
I mean, maybe a musician who died.

Well, I might have done that, but I wasn't here when the musician died. And, yeah, that would have been a different situation. But anyway, it was just a total stranger. I didn't think it. My sensibilities were such that I cut myself off at that point and I wouldn't follow them into the cemetery.
Well, I have marched with a family at a funeral, you know, which is a little different, but, you know, I was asked to do that.
Yeah.
And it seems like so many musicians have died since you were here in the 50s.
Well, I gather now that that's about the only time you really have a jazz funeral is when a musician dies.
No, they have other times.
Do they? Yeah.
There's a lot of stuff going on that you don't hear about.
Yeah.
But it's, the second line has really gotten unruly.
Yeah.
Did you ever see them get really unruly?
No.
Misbehaved? Never? No. That's interesting.

They were always on the sidewalk, close to the band, you know, up next to it. They would surge back and forth, but I've never seen them get unruly and I've never seen them really interfere in any way with the procession itself, the progress of the thing.
They didn't bump into the trombone player and knock his teeth out.
No. No. No. No. No, indeed. Nothing like that.
I don't remember a lot of fights or anything like that.

I don't remember ever seeing a fight. That's one of the striking things to me, going to those parades, that they would fill the streets and they would have these huge second lines, but there never seemed to be any real, any angry people or any really sort of conflict. It was something that people just sort of shared in and enjoyed. And I'm amused now, too, to see these second lines that get tricked up for the bands that play down the French Quarter and other places, where they have these umbrellas that have precise frills all around them in different colors. That is just so totally away from what those second lines were 30 years ago. They had umbrellas, but the ideal one would be nothing but ribs and a few tatters of black umbrella fabric hanging down. And to have one of those really frilly, fancy ones, it just seems very alien to me.
It's very phony to me. Sometimes people would come out and look like they deliberately dressed down, shall we say, and would get a beat-up umbrella.
Oh, yeah. The more beat-up it was, I think the more desirable it was.
No fabric at all.
Yeah, just the bare ribs. Yeah. I don't want to forget this.
We've talked so much about the brass bands. Tell me about going to here in my hair, Joe. Oh, okay.

Yeah. You did want to make sure. Well, again, I don't remember exactly what year that was. It was, my guess is it was 58, but it might have been 57. But I remember that I first became aware of it when riding on the Fred Street bus and seeing notices on telephone poles and in record shops, placards, that she was going to be here. And so I, you know, we might have not talked about it. We certainly would like to go and hear her do that. And so we made our plans to do so. She was going to sing on a Sunday, I believe, at the Municipal Auditorium. And we went down early because we had not bought tickets ahead of time and had to stand in a long line. We were two white faces in a great sea of black people that were waiting to buy tickets and got up to the ticket window and bought tickets. I was thinking about this a couple of days ago that I don't remember what they cost, but I do remember they were expensive. You know, that I felt like I was, as a graduate student, didn't have much cash money and that I was making a special effort to buy those more. It was costing me. It cost a hell of a lot more than going to a movie or something, you know. It was a big expenditure. And so we bought our tickets and went on into the building. And there's a black man there who took our tickets up and greeted us cordially and said, Come on in, white folks, sit anywhere you like. And we went on in and got another 50 feet. And the white New Orleans policeman grabbed me by the arm and said, You know, where do you think you're going? And I said, Well, I want to go in here to hear Bahia Jackson sing. And he said, You can't come in here. And so I remonstrated with him a little bit and went, you know, it was pretty clear that he wasn't going to let us in. And you say you don't remember this, but about that time you came walking by following in the wake of some black woman who had a ribbon on it that said committee. And you were carrying an arm load of what looked like printed programs for the occasion. And by that time it was clear I was going to be thrown out. And I thought, Aha, how clever Dick Allen is that he has gotten in by assuming this official role in the service of the committee woman. But the policeman let me go back to the box office to get my money back. But then I thought more and thought, Well, I want to talk to the manager. So we went to the manager's office. And by the time we got there, there were six or eight other white people there who also had been thrown out. And there are various states of anger. Everybody is yelling at the manager of the place. About that time you appeared in the manager's office. And Bill Russell was there by then too. Some people were just sort of quietly trying to persuade the guy to let him in after all. And others were denouncing the whole system and claiming their constitutional rights and threatening lawsuits. And the manager was just saying, I have no control over it whatsoever. The promoters are the ones. And if they will designate an area for white people to sit in, we can let you in. But they have not set aside a space for white people. And you can't go in until they do. And so we eventually got somebody who was a promoter or the promoter's assistant to come over there and talk to us. And he again reiterated his welcome and said, we're just delighted to have you. Come sit anywhere you want to. But he would not designate a special section of the auditorium for white people. And as much as I wanted to hear Mahalia Jackson sing, I admired his stand on it. And he wasn't going to be bullied and shoved down. And so the manager just refused to let us in. And Bill Russell gathered you and I think Ida and I followed along with you. And I think Irvin Helfer was there too, as I think back on that.
Better than.

And it was just that tiny little night. There was not all the white people who were in the manager's office who went out with Bill Russell. And he said, we'll go around and see if we can't go in the stage door and stand in the wings. And he knew Mahalia Jackson or she knew him. They were acquainted well. And his idea was that he would get permission for him and his friends to come in and stand in the wings and hear us sing. So we went back to the stage door and hung around outside and messages went in and out. And finally her brother came out and spoke to us. And somebody told me he was her brother. And he apparently lived in New Orleans and she was living in Chicago by that time, I think. And he was kind of a ne'er-do-well, I gather. But he became a messenger. He at first was reluctant to even take the message in to his sister from Bill Russell because he didn't want to upset her. But finally he did take a message in. And all of that was to no avail. At one point he came out and said that he had brought the message from Mahalia Jackson that it hurt her in the heart that Bill Russell and her friends couldn't hear her sing in New Orleans. But we finally gave up and went away. Walked back down to Morning Call and had a cup of coffee and some beignets. And I felt very much discriminated against. It's the only time in my life that I remember being discriminated against by the color of my skin. And the black promoter certainly struck a blow for integration with me, the way you handled the whole thing.
Well that was Russell's feeling. I can remember discussing it with Russell later.
Yeah.
But I don't remember the details of going into the auditorium and all that.
Yeah.
And the program.

Well, I remember. Yeah. You look smug as hell walking along with a hum full of programs. And then there's something else that I just remembered the other day when I was thinking about this. And it has nothing to do with the Mahalia Jackson concert. And I remember that as we were walking away from the minister of the auditorium and going back down in the French Quarter to sort of grumble, that we passed by a group of people who were playing some game, a ball game or something. And you were telling me that this was a traditional weekend activity and that that game had been going on for generations or something. Do you remember anything about that?
It was being played in Jackson Square?
Yeah. No, no, no, in Congo Square.
In Congo Square. In Borgo Square.
Borgo, yeah.
White guys with baseballs and bats.
Yeah.
Called tree ball. And it was a variation of baseball. And they had their own ground rules, I guess you could say.
Yeah.
But how can you have ground rules for the trees?
But that was a New Orleans tradition that had been going there for years.

Yeah, it had been going on for years. Yeah. They had a very strange game. Of course, there were all kinds of stuff like that going on in this town. All kinds of sports in New Orleans were very different in some ways.
Yeah.
But that's before my time, most of that stuff. And I don't want to get away from the music and everything. Except to ask, what type of history do you teach?
I teach modern European history.
Modern European.
된 stuff
And you have a good memory after the time.

I came up here when my daughter was here earlier this week, and her friend wanted to visit the archives and see what displays were up here. And I did look at the pictures that I had sent down here and that you had looked at. And again, I was interested that in those pictures that I had taken, and that was a big parade in, I think it was probably 56 or 57. There were five bands in that parade, I remember, that I had tried to take pictures that included not only the band but the marches. And that is one of the pictures that shows a band marching down between. They were at the Booker T. Washington Auditorium, I think, and they had formed the paraders as they got there had formed a column that the oncoming marches marched in between. And all the women went white dresses and little red hats and all that. In my youth, I had tried to capture the setting and not just the band. I was proud of myself for having done that.
Were you here for Mardi Gras?

Oh, yeah, sure. We were here, several Mardi Gras. I don't remember any music particularly at Mardi Gras. And I did not really get hooked on Mardi Gras. But I could hardly, would hardly have spent three years in New Orleans and not experienced that part of the city's life. Part of it. Yeah. Good stuff.

When I came back, was here in the summer of 1965 for about a week when I finally finished my degree and I came down to attend my own commencement to receive my Ph.D. degree. And that so happened that while we were here, somebody died who was the business manager of one of the bands. And I don't remember what band it was, and I don't remember who he was. But I remember seeing the obituary in the paper, and he was an important enough musician to have had a picture in the paper. And I asked you, having seen the thing, I thought, gee, there'll probably be a funeral, and I called you up. And you did nothing about it then, but a couple days later got back in touch, and indeed there was a jazz funeral for him. And I went and saw that one. And even that was in 55. The whole thing had changed a little bit from what it... In 65. In 65, yeah.
It had changed from what it had been eight, nine years earlier when I experienced it. Do you remember A.B. Spears?
No. Who was A.B. Spears?
He was the manager and to the saxophonist with the E. Gibson brass band.
Yeah, that might have been it.
I don't know why.

I think of him as the other one. That might have been... The guy was a saxophone player, if you believe. That might have been who it was. One of the things that I remember, but going to that parade at one point, there was a little handful of white people who were there, that one of the musicians spotted me and came over and spoke to me and acted as if he knew me. And I didn't disabuse him. But it turns out that really he remembered seeing me on the streets when I had been here ten years ago, and I was a familiar face. And so we talked about that and reminisced a little bit. And I don't remember what his name was either, but he kept telling me that he had a place across the lake in Mandeville. And would I please want me to come over and have a barbecue?
Chuck Fortier. Yeah. He was always telling me that, and I never will.
He is kind of a funny guy. But I do remember that... Yeah.
A saxophone player.
Yeah. That at the end, at that parade, when they got to the point where they were going to the burying ground, that instead of marching, the hearse was there in the car and had a big motorcade.
Mm-hmm.
And they went roaring down the street while the band stood on the street and played. And they disappeared into the distance. That was the end of the occasion.
You never heard a band at a wedding or anything like that, huh? No. No. I'm trying to think of any non-union brass bands that were around.
I didn't know any of them were unions then.
Yeah. It was my impression, and I think you told me one time when I asked you,

what John Casimir and the Young Tuxedo used to get for playing those bands and those jobs, a large parade or whatever. And I remember that at one point you said they got five bucks a piece and at least they got ten. But whether you were just stringing me along... Oh, no. ...or whether that was an authentic... Was that a reunion rate on it?
Yeah, but they had special rates for funerals, and they'd give you a funeral rate for a short parade.
Uh-huh.
And I don't know why there was such a great funeral.

You know, I always thought that was sort of pitiful that they didn't get paid more for their work. And that when I did come back for my graduation, by that time Preservation Hall was going, and I had never been down there, so I went down to hear that. And I had really real mixed feelings at that time about the whole thing. I liked the idea that the musicians were there and could get a payday and get paid and have an audience, but I also thought that the music had deteriorated something awful, that it was... And again, maybe that was the fact that I had not had a lot of familiarity with them playing, sort of sitting down with a piano in a concert setting as opposed to playing in the streets with a brass band. But I thought it had gotten that they grandstanded for the audience right much and that the music had suffered in the process. Whether that was just some sort of prejudice bond of nostalgia on my part, I really don't know, but I was disappointed in it. And I still really don't like Preservation Hall that much, I think.
I don't know. No. We're about to run out of tape, so I'll pose a question. We can answer it when it runs through. If you have time to do another reel.
Oh, if you want to do another reel.
Yeah, one more. Okay. Reel 3, John Wood. 26th of June, 1986. Is that right? That's correct. Where are we, anyhow, John?
Where are we?
Yeah.
We're in the William R. Hogan Jazz Archive in the Howard Tilton Library.
That's pretty good.
That's close enough.
Tulane University of Louisiana. Tulane University.
Yeah.
All right. We're going to talk about your having records.

Okay. I don't have many records, and I don't think that I have but two that I can really identify as going back to the 50s. One is a record that someone named Irvin Helfer produced when he was an undergraduate called Primitive Piano, and he went off and recorded, made tapes of, it must be four or five, maybe six different piano players that he's got on the record. Billy Pierce is one that he's got on there.
Yeah. Some of them he recorded himself, and some of them he got from somebody else, you know, things like that.
Yeah.
But it was an interesting record.

I've still got that. And then there's another record that I have, and I think I must have bought it before I left New Orleans when I was through being in graduate school, and it's this Atlantic recording of the young Tuxedo Brass Band called Jazz Begins. Was that produced in 58, 59, 58? Yeah. Yeah. I've got that, and I have, that's a continuing pleasure to me. I still play that record a lot. And I was intrigued when I was down here last summer to hear a band one afternoon playing down at the gazebo, and when they introduced the members of the band, that one of them was named Wendell Brunius, and so after they were finished playing, I went over and engaged him in conversation and found out that, yes, indeed, he was the son of the man who used to play the trumpet in the young Tuxedo Brass Band, and that I remembered that they had recorded that Atlantic record, part of it at least, at the band playing outside in John Brunius' backyard, and Wendell pointed out to me that his picture is on the album, that the photograph has a little kid in it, and he's the little kid that they took of the bandstand in the backyard. So I thought that was really, it was a nice sort of link and continuity for me, and I enjoyed hearing him play, and since I've been down here this summer, I've enjoyed hearing him play, and I enjoyed him sing. I didn't realize until last Sunday that he also does a lot of vocals, but, and he's been very cordial and very pleasant to me. I think of him as a friend, really. And I bought his record the other night. I took it home. I haven't played it yet, but somebody told me it's really not a bad record,
so I'm glad to have that.

And then I did buy some records when I was down here in the summer of 65 to graduate, and I was kind of bewildered, because by that time, there were Preservation Hall record labels available, and there were a lot of records that I had never, I guess these recordings had been done, and I didn't have but so much money, and I didn't know which records to buy. But I did buy two that I, three, really, that I remember that I still cherish. One is a record that features John Casimir. It's got his picture on the cover.
Is that with his sit-down band or his brass band?
It's his brass band, I think. No, it's with the sit-down band.
Okay.
And it was done after he, I believe, you know, that the liner notes, whoever wrote them, were written after he died. When did he die? Do you know?
No, I haven't.
Early 60s sometime, probably.
Right in there. Yeah.
The other one,
I have a bad memory for dates and all that.

It was a record that features Jim Robinson, and I asked you about it, I think, and it's under the Pearl label, and you told me that that was his, named it that because it's his wife's name. That's right. Yeah.
It's the one that's got Kid Thomas and Ernie Cagnolite both on trumpet.
Yeah. They played it,
I Will Be Somewhere Working for the Lord.

Yeah, that's a good record, and I like that one. And then the other one that I have that I bought that same summer, is a Kid Howard record that was all hymns, and is recorded in the Zion Hill Baptist Church. And it starts off with a little welcome by the preacher, the minister of the church. I'm the Reverend Alexander Griffin, or whatever, and I want to welcome all these people. And that's, I enjoy that. But those, you know, I really, and last summer, again, is a bewildering array of records, and you don't know how to buy one. It's going to be any good. You can't listen to them ahead of time. And I bought several records. To my shame, I let them get warped in my car. It got too hot. But the one that I did buy, and I enjoyed a lot, but it's badly warped, is a George Lewis record of him playing hymns with just piano play and bass, I guess. A record you had something to do with.
Yeah. Well, that narrows it down. Yeah.

And, in fact, when my daughter was here earlier this week, we did go down to Preservation Hall one night, and there was one copy of that record still in the back bin, and I bought it to replace my warped one, and I bought them. That one, the Brunius one down there, too. And last time, I also bought the Kid Thomas record that has Sammy Remington on it, which Kid Thomas plays Red Wing. I bought it because I like that number, and I thought it's... Who is Sammy Remington? Yeah, he appears. I see his name on all these records that are down there. Is the name of him? And I don't know him at all.
Yeah, and he plays clarinet, usually. And he sounds a lot like George Lewis as a way of characterizing it.
And so he's helped with this recording. I mean, he's pushed recording a lot.
Yeah.
Well, it's pretty bewildering to confront all those records and not to know which one to buy and what have you.
I just wondered how much the later records reflected the musical things.

I don't... They're not much. Really. And, you know, even that... I've heard other records that I've bought in other places that, you know, alleged to be New Orleans brass bands playing for funerals and stuff. And none of it really, I think, is very good. That that Atlantic record of the Young Tuxedo comes the closest. But even that lacks something. I think when they get moving down the street, they pick up the rhythm better. And it's different when you're out there actually marching down the street playing when you're trying to stand and play for somebody's recording equipment, even if you are outside in somebody's backyard trying to do it. But again, I don't know enough about the nuances of the music and the technical differences of one band to another to be a real critic. But I do think... I do personally just enjoy that Atlantic record very much because it does come closest to capturing the sound that I used to hear in the streets of anything I've heard so far. And that's not to say there are not other records out there that do a better job of it, but I'm just not familiar with them. I would like to know about them if they're there.
What about the radio?
The radio?
Do you ever hear anything on the radio?
Down in the 50s, practically nothing.
I haven't even thought about that.
I'm not sure, but didn't... The New Orleans Jazz Club used to maybe have a weekly program or something, and Dr. Suchon used to do
some radio programs occasionally.
But you hear, it seems to me, much more on the radio now than you did then.
Well, do the records on the radio sound anything that... Do you hear anything that pleases you particularly?
Oh, yeah. A lot of them please me, but they are not... Excuse me. You don't hear so much of the brass band sound. But I just... I... enjoy WHO's... stuff

O.Z. And on Saturday mornings, when I'm down here, I lie in bed and listen to Big Mama Betty Rank and do her hour and a half and enjoy it very much usually. And then other times when I can find, when I'm not in class and they're playing something. But it is, one of my frustrations being down here the past couple of summers is that I don't have with me equipment, you know, a simple cassette recorder that I could record right off the radio.
Yeah.
But I think, you know, real often, gee, you know, gosh, I really wish I had something like that. I could take that home and play it a lot and enjoy it.
You don't find too many of those records in Virginia.
No, I don't think you do.
No. I don't think you do. Do you remember the George Williams brass band?

Well, I heard them on the streets a couple of times. They were not there a lot. And whenever they were there, I remember, you know, that people would say, oh, you know, like Irvin Helfer would say, gee, we really want to make sure we go and hear them. That's all. But other than the fact that I know they were there, and in fact they were this set of pictures that I gave you, there's one I have, they were in that, they were in that parade. But I don't have any real recollection of any sort of distinctive sound or playing that they were doing.
You don't remember that they were better or worse than the Eureka?
Oh, I think they were worse than the Eureka and the Young Tuxedo, which were the two that were really, I thought, the best two bands that we heard.
Well, most, so do I, but Bill Russell, for example, liked the George Williams battle.
Yeah.
Of course, they had a clarinet in there, and he liked that clarinet player, I guess.

I remember now that you were talking about multiple bands that there were a couple of occasions when, for Sunday school parades, when they got to the Booker T. Washington Auditorium and the marches in the parade had to walk up these long steps to get into the big double doors, that the first band in the parade would pull off and stand at the foot of the steps and play, and as the other bands caught up, they would have this masked band effect, and by the time the whole parade was in, there'd be, on one occasion, there were five bands that were there playing all together, playing when the Saints go marching in, and, you know, it would go on for a long time because it was a long parade, and it took a long time for everybody to get up the steps and inside the hall, and that was pretty exciting music. One occasion, I remember two of the bass horn players, tuba players, Wilbert Tillman was one of them, and I don't know who the other person was, but they were playing in this masked band thing, and they were standing just facing each other, practically bell to bell, and they were just having a wonderful time trying to blow each other off the street. And they would, one would play a little phrase, and the other would pick it up and blow it right back at them, and at the other one, they'd trade things back and forth, and when one would do a particularly hard sequence, or they liked the way it'd all come out, they'd stop and throw their heads back and just laugh like hell,
and then play some more.
They were having a wonderful time trying to blow each other off the street, and it was quite a display.
Did you get the feeling that all the bands were organized, all the brass bands, or, you know, that...

Well, I guess my feeling was that they were... that they didn't always show up with the same people, obviously, but that there was a basic organization there, there was a basic membership, and that there was somebody that was in charge of sort of looking out and getting it all organized, and that it was an organization that had some continuity to it. I maybe didn't understand what all that was there, but my impression was that the Eurik and the Young Tuxedo in particular had been there for a long, long time, and that there were people that were playing with it that had been playing with it for a long, long time. As I remember, who was the guy? Emil Knox. He played drums with them. He was a fairly old guy. He'd been playing with them for a long, long time. But, you know, I don't really remember... They were...
They probably played eight or ten pieces in those bands, and, you know, ten.
And, you know, John Casimir was always there, and I remember Jim Robinson was almost always in the band, and Wilbur Tillman was always, almost always in it.

I was just thinking, at a big Sunday school parade, they might have had some bands. You know, they had so many bands, they might have had some bands that would jump up bands, as they called them. Yeah.

I'm, you know, I wasn't aware of that, and I guess it always, it would surprise me that there would be a band like the George Williams band. I had been going parades for a year, year and a half, and had never heard of it, and all of a sudden, there it is, you know, and it's got a drum, and it's got George Williams painted on it, and everything, and so, you know, that, that doesn't mean a whole lot, I guess. But, I remember like Barry Ratton, a couple of weeks ago, had a big banner up, it's embroidered, and it looks very, it says a pelican, jazz band, or whatever, and, you know, that's, it turns out, that's his personal banner, that's all-purpose banner, that he puts up whenever he plays, and the personnel of the band varies considerably, from one time to another, but I think at those bands in the 50s, there was probably more continuity of personnel, that they were identifiably a member of a given band, and while there were substitutions, and people, they play around from one band to another, that people were thought of as being a member of this band, or that band, that may well still be the case, I don't really know.
I was thinking about, we mentioned Irwin, did the students have any parties?
Well, if they did, I was a married graduate student, and I don't remember ever going to a party, You didn't go to a party with a band? Where there was live music, no, no.
Did people ever pass the hat, or ask for contributions anyway?

The only time, certainly not the brass bands, that played in the street, that I went to, never. I know the only extra contribution, that I remember being involved in, is when you made a request, at the paddock lounge, you'd throw them a couple of bucks,

and they would play a number for you, but I don't remember anybody. You weren't asked to buy a ticket, to any church function? No. I have seen, something I haven't seen in years, but, four people carrying a sheet, one in each corner. And ask people to throw money, and you throw money in it,
as they go by. I never saw, I don't remember seeing that, in any of the parades. Well then how do you know it?
Well I've seen it in other places, that they would,
you know,
volunteer,
fire department parades,
and stuff like that,
at home, they'll do that. But I don't recall, ever seeing anybody, soliciting, your contribution, at one of those, occasions.
Tell me about, Decatur Street.
Then?
Then? Did you go to, Decatur Street in the 50's? I don't remember,

never heard music on Decatur Street. You know, Decatur Street in the 50's, the French market was, you know, it was a real fish market, and Battistellas, and those other people, had those great big tables, and shrimp were piled up on, and fish, and everything, and fruits, and vegetables. And, but I, don't remember, ever going to music, on Decatur Street. I may have missed, it completely. There was a place, down there, called Ruggiero's, it was kind of, a Siemens hangout, that had imported, German beer, and used to go in there, and drink spot, and dark spot, and brow beer, but it's not there, anymore either.
No.
He used to have, good stuffed crab, and had a barbershop, in the back. Charles Davis, and I used to go down there, he would speak Italian, with the proprietor, and he would knock 15% off the bill.
Oh, good. Well, these last few summers, you say five summers, you've been here.
Yeah.
Have you gone to, Decatur Street, from the beginning?

Just sort of, wandered by, and to the, to the gazebo, and to the, Cafe Mediterranean, you know, I usually wander over there, and listen to what's going on, after I've heard, whatever's at the tent, and sometimes, the music is really, pretty good. Sometimes, I don't like it much. It depends, maybe on, my mood, and maybe how many beers, I've had, by the afternoon, and where it's on, but, then at the gazebo, some of that music, is pretty good. I've enjoyed, John Royan's piano playing, right much down there, and, I don't know, what is it, that, the fellow's name, that plays the clarinet down there, who's an Englishman, been around for a while. Chris Burke. Chris Burke, wears his hair, kind of in a bang,
in the front. That's him, yeah. No, no, I just wondered, how that compared, with the music, of years gone by, if any of the bands, down there, sound like the old-timey band.
I don't think so.
At the gazebo? Yeah. Or, Cafe Mediterranean. Or the tent. Yeah,

the tent bands, sometimes do. They don't sound like, well, I guess, the only band, that I've heard down there, that really builds itself, as a brass band, was, three weeks ago, this summer, I think it was, the Onward Brass Band,
was down there.
No,
not, yeah, that's it.
Dijans, oh, the Olympia, not the Onward, the Olympia Brass.
And, you know,

I don't really enjoy them, particularly, although I was kind of interested, they had, the Junior Olympia Brass Band, and all these little kids, and it was kind of fun, to see those little kids play. Some guy, a little bitty guy, must have been, no more than nine, ten years old, really get a lot of sound, out of the trumpet. But then, a couple, weeks later, walking down Bourbon Street, they were up, playing it on the street, and passing the hat, the, you know, but, you know, that setting, that concert setting, is, is really not the same, ambience, as, as the whole thing was. I have enjoyed, very much, hearing, some of those concerts, down in the, in the, at the tent, in the French Quarter. Last summer, I remember hearing, Chester's artists play, that was, just a wonderful, musical afternoon, down there. and then, the group that was there, last, Sunday. But that, you know, that's an orchestra, not a brass band.
Yes.

But, I love the music, and I, I like the, the, really, I like the traditional, music, um, over at the Café Mediterranean, that is just a little too hokey for me, that's too, too, too tourist, uh, oriented, somehow, or all. I just don't really.
The French Market Jazz Band, you're talking about. Yeah, is that what it's called? Scott Hill. I assume that's who you're talking about.
Yeah, and Greg Stafford plays with them.
Yeah.
Yeah.
The Lita's a blonde trombone player.
Yeah.
Yeah. I guess middle age. Yeah. They have a woman playing band.

Yeah. Amy, what her name is. Sure. She, she wasn't there last Sunday. You know, it's, it's fine, it's, it's okay, but it somehow falls a little short. Uh, I wouldn't want to, I wouldn't spend three hours sitting listening to them.
Well, how, how, how, are they louder than the ragtime orchestra? Is it like ragtime orchestra louder than them?
Oh, I don't know. Oh, loudness. What kind of yardstick is that?
I don't know. I mean, that's one thing. Yeah. Some people play fast,
some people play loud. Well, I like it not so loud and not so fast.
Yeah.
And, uh, so the ragtime orchestra is not playing that loud. Mm-hmm. And, and, while they do play fast sometimes, there are things,
you know,

to me, the, one of the things that I really like, oh, respond to, and, you know, my, sort of perception of the traditional New Orleans music is, that, while it is fast, it's never frantic, it's never frenetic. Uh, they never get, sort of, uh, it's always has, even at its most exuberant, it has a certain sort of, uh, polite restraint to it, almost.
Yeah.

Uh, and they never lose sight, uh, of the melody, you know, they never get so far from the melody line, that you're just sort of lost in the improvisation, that they do. Uh, it's an accessible music, to me, you know, and that it is, it's direct, and it's articulate, and, uh, it, uh, is, is, is, is accessible, I think is maybe a, a good word, uh, but, uh, and so, I never have liked these.

you know, like the Dukes of Dixieland and things like that, because it always seems to me that they are just, they lack a depth and sort of an emotional dimension that the traditional bands, I thought, seem to have. That is a certain vacuity in what they're playing. They're just sort of going through the motions sometimes. That may be a harsh judgment and an unfair judgment, but, you know, that's my perception.
Well, I mean, to stick it to the ragtime orchestra, do you think of them as a jazz band?
Well, again, you're getting kind of technical, and I guess no, not really, you know, that it's a dance orchestra. Well, jazz is not ragtime, or is it? I don't know. I don't know.
I mean, the thing is that I'm just wondering about it.
What makes jazz?
They're sitting there reading a lot of the time.
Yeah. Well, I used to, some of the brass bands that played in the street used to read. They would have music mounted on their music stands on their home. But not to that extent. No, no.
I mean, this seems to me to be a very different band, and it achieves a very different sound.
Yeah.
And they've gone back and dug out things. Do you feel like they're copying records?
No.
I don't feel that either.
I don't feel that. And I think that, you know, that's what they're doing is a very legitimate sort of extension of an earlier musical tradition.
Yeah.

And I find that it's very enjoyable, but it's certainly not the brass band tradition, and it's not certainly a long, long ways from a Bourbon Street sort of jazz set, that kind of tradition. But it's, and I'm not a jazz historian, and you are, and you can put that, you know, ragtime orchestra in its proper context and proper setting.
Well, it's your reaction to it that I'm getting at. Yeah. Yeah.

Well, it falls within this sort of, you know, perimeter of things that I like, is that it is direct and accessible, and it is not frantic, and they don't play a lot of dissident chords, and they play in tune pretty much. That's good. Well, we could overlook a few that.
Go ahead.

But it has that certain sort of accessible restrained quality about it. At the same time, it flows very freely, and it's open, and it's in many ways very joyous. And now I find that all that's very appealing. Very appealing, indeed.
Well, I just wondered if you noticed how much improvising there was.
Well, not a lot, and they don't do a lot of solo work either, do they?
Yeah. It strikes me that they have a few tunes which they play, which are entirely played by here. Yeah. But they didn't do much of that Sunday. Yeah.
Do they play as a group fairly regularly, or is it kind of unusual for them to come together and do a concert like this?
It's unusual, and they would go on a tour and then play regularly.
Yeah.

But I think they do, on the whole, put a New Orleans interpretation on things. Sure. You know, it's not just the reading the music, because there are other bands that read those same arrangements, and they come out.
Come out differently.
Oh, very differently.
Yeah. Not going to be.
Well, let me see what else. I was going to ask you if you remember hearing any street cries.

I guess I do remember maybe somebody coming through selling strawberries uptown in the strawberry season. But, you know, it was an unusual thing. They were not a part of the scene when I was here in the 50s, at least of the scene that I was aware of.
If it was done, it was done in another neighborhood.
Yeah.
I was really wondering if you heard, also if you heard different things in different neighborhoods, but obviously not. Did anybody speak any Creole then?

Occasionally I remember, you know, you say Creole, I don't really know what you mean by that. I remember being, for instance, in the cafeteria line at Morrison's Cafeteria, and being behind a family of parents and a couple of little children, who were obviously New Orleans residents, and they were all conversing in French, and I found that, you know, caught my attention. But I don't remember a lot of that cultural side of New Orleans. I had no real reason to be into it.
Another thing I was wondering about, like the Eureka back in the 50s, who do you remember from the band then?
You know, Dick, I really can't tell you. I can't remember. The only band whose personnel I really distinctly remember is the Young Tuxedo, and that was in part because that was my favorite band.
Yeah. Well, that's interesting to me.
And, you know, I used to hear the Eureka Valley regularly, but I can't tell you. Did Paul Barberin play with them regularly? No, he played with something called the Onward Brass Band.
Yeah, he had formed the Onward. Yeah. But that was later.

That was later. I guess I heard them again when I came down here to graduate. That's when I heard them. That could be. He was playing at a place on Bourbon Street that was competing Dixieland Hall or something. Yeah. It was kind of another version of Preservation Hall, and I remember hearing them. But, you know, no, I can't. I remember hearing the Eureka on the streets a lot, but who played with them? Tell me some names.
Well, do you know Percy Humphrey?
Did he play with them?
Yeah, he was the leader.
He was the leader.
He was the one with the little sack on his shoulder carrying all the music.

Yeah. Well, you know, speaking of that, Percy Humphrey, that reminds me of something else that I wanted to tell you about. That in, it would have been in the late 60s, I guess, in my little community of Harrisonburg, Virginia, which is nearby a place called Bridgewater, which has Bridgewater College. And I thought that Bridgewater College sponsored an appearance of a Preservation Hall jazz band in February one year. And these signs went up, and I was excited about that. And when the day came for their performance, I thought it was a February day, and it was really cold. It was about 10 degrees. And I thought I would go to the motel and just try to speak to the musicians and some of them and extend the word of will. Thank you very much. Thank you.

segments.chapter: Opening and background
segments.title: Opening: name, date and recording check
segments.summary: Allen checks the recorder and Wood gives his name, home town and the date.

segments.chapter: Opening and background
segments.title: Wood's background, Army service and early exposure to jazz
segments.summary: Born in Richmond in 1928, drafted in 1951, taught at Tulane and JMU; recalls Lead Belly records, Mister Jelly Roll, and meeting drummer Paul Barbarin at his first parade.

segments.chapter: Brass band parades in the 1950s
segments.title: Sunday school parades, Shakespeare Park and the first parade
segments.summary: They recall Sunday school parades from Shakespeare Park to Booker T. Washington Auditorium, renamed places, and dating the first parade to summer 1956.

segments.chapter: Brass band parades in the 1950s
segments.title: How Wood and Allen met; which band Barbarin played with
segments.summary: Wood says they met through the Tulane history department and Hogan; they guess Barbarin was with Eureka or Young Tuxedo, with substitutes common.

segments.chapter: Brass band parades in the 1950s
segments.title: Competing bands at parades, then and now
segments.summary: Wood describes bands alternating and the frustration of running between them, compared with the June 1986 parade with two distant bands and embroidered hats.

segments.chapter: Parade of June 1986 and Young Tuxedo today
segments.title: The revived Young Tuxedo compared with the 1950s band
segments.summary: Wood heard the revived Tuxedo and Chosen Few bands on 21 June 1986 and says the sound differs from John Casimir's band, including the brass bass and growling runs.
