segments.chapter: Parade of June 1986 and Young Tuxedo today
segments.title: Greg Stafford and Barry Wratten on tradition
segments.summary: Stafford gave Wood a ride and objected to a non-New Orleanian speaking authoritatively about the tradition; he said the music must grow but stay in the tradition.

segments.chapter: Parade of June 1986 and Young Tuxedo today
segments.title: No second line at the 1986 parade, versus the 1950s
segments.summary: Wood notes almost no second line at the June 1986 parade and contrasts it with the joyous umbrella-waving kids of the late 1950s.

segments.chapter: Parade of June 1986 and Young Tuxedo today
segments.title: Floats, cars and the church behind the 1986 parade
segments.summary: Wood describes floats, a school marching band, dignitaries in cars, and the AME church pre-bicentennial celebration.

segments.chapter: Brass band parades in the 1950s
segments.title: The June 1958 parade on Hamburg Street and church hymns
segments.summary: They discuss a 22 June 1958 Young Tuxedo parade before a church service, where Wood asked Allen the name of 'Just a Closer Walk' and enjoyed hymns played by brass bands.

segments.chapter: Brass band parades in the 1950s
segments.title: Wood's church background and rural Virginia roots
segments.summary: Wood moved from Baptist to Presbyterian to Episcopalian, explains his Fluvanna County roots, and Allen mentions Paul Crawford's hymn knowledge.

segments.chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
segments.title: Feeling like an intruder at black neighborhood parades
segments.summary: Wood felt a white stranger in a black neighborhood but was never made unwelcome, and recalls being pulled into a second line.

segments.chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
segments.title: Funeral music, the marshal and John Casimir's tears
segments.summary: Funeral bands switched from fast warm-up numbers to slow marches, the marshal set the mood, and Casimir wept while playing clarinet.

segments.chapter: Being a white observer, funerals and second lines
segments.title: Tape change to Reel 2
segments.summary: Allen announces Reel 2 and corrects the date to 1986.

segments.chapter: Wratten's band and the Paddock Lounge
segments.title: Barry Wratten's band in the French Market
segments.summary: Wood heard Wratten's band on 15 June, was moved by 'Just a Closer Walk With Thee', and discusses the loud amplified guitar and Wratten's view of early guitar levels.

segments.chapter: Wratten's band and the Paddock Lounge
segments.title: Current Young Tuxedo plans; Paddock Lounge and Bill Matthews
segments.summary: Wood notes the grapevine and more music than he expected, and recalls the Paddock Lounge and the Bill Matthews band as his only non-brass-band music in the 1950s.

segments.chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
segments.title: Not going to dance halls
segments.summary: Wood never went to dance halls, feeling an intruder; Allen explains that black dance halls rarely hired old-time jazz bands except for parades.

segments.chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
segments.title: Band serenades an old man in a wheelchair
segments.summary: Wood recounts a parade that stopped at a shotgun house to honour an elderly man, and the band not being invited to the lodge hall.

segments.chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
segments.title: Waiting outside funerals; never following to the cemetery
segments.summary: Wood fraternized with musicians over beer while services ran, and never followed a funeral into the cemetery.

segments.chapter: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
segments.title: Jazz funerals today, orderly second lines and umbrellas
segments.summary: They discuss funerals for musicians, Wood never saw second lines unruly or fights, and contrasts tattered umbrellas then with fancy ones now.

segments.chapter: Mahalia Jackson concert and Congo Square
segments.title: Turned away from the Mahalia Jackson concert
segments.summary: In 1957-58 Wood and his wife were stopped by a policeman at the Municipal Auditorium, argued with the manager, and Bill Russell tried the stage door without success.

segments.chapter: Mahalia Jackson concert and Congo Square
segments.title: Congo Square tree ball game
segments.summary: Walking away, they passed a traditional ball game in Congo Square, which Allen identifies as tree ball.

segments.chapter: Mahalia Jackson concert and Congo Square
segments.title: Wood's teaching, his parade photographs and Mardi Gras
segments.summary: Wood teaches modern European history and describes photographs of a 1956-57 parade with five bands; he remembers no Mardi Gras music.

segments.chapter: Return in 1965, pay and Preservation Hall
segments.title: Returning in 1965 for a jazz funeral
segments.summary: Wood returned in 1965 for his degree and attended a funeral for a band manager, where the hearse drove off while the band played, and a saxophonist (Chuck Fortier) invited him to Mandeville.

segments.chapter: Return in 1965, pay and Preservation Hall
segments.title: Union status and pay for brass band jobs
segments.summary: They discuss whether bands were union and what Casimir and Young Tuxedo were paid, five or ten dollars, with funeral rates.

segments.chapter: Return in 1965, pay and Preservation Hall
segments.title: Impressions of Preservation Hall in 1965
segments.summary: Wood was glad the musicians were paid but felt the music grandstanded for audiences and still does not like Preservation Hall much.

segments.chapter: Records and radio
segments.title: Reel 3 begins; location and topic
segments.summary: Allen announces Reel 3 and they state the interview location at the Hogan Jazz Archive.

segments.chapter: Records and radio
segments.title: Records from the 1950s: Primitive Piano and Jazz Begins
segments.summary: Wood owns Irvin Helfer's Primitive Piano and the Atlantic Young Tuxedo record, and met Wendell Brunious, whose father played trumpet on it.

segments.chapter: Records and radio
segments.title: Records bought in 1965 and 1986
segments.summary: Wood bought records of John Casimir, Jim Robinson, Kid Howard, George Lewis and Kid Thomas, and finds Preservation Hall labels bewildering.

segments.chapter: Records and radio
segments.title: How well records capture the street sound
segments.summary: Wood says few records capture brass bands well and the Atlantic Young Tuxedo album comes closest.

segments.chapter: Records and radio
segments.title: Radio then and now
segments.summary: Wood heard almost no jazz on radio in the 1950s and now enjoys WWOZ and a Saturday morning host.

segments.chapter: Bands and membership
segments.title: George Williams brass band versus Eureka and Young Tuxedo
segments.summary: Wood heard the George Williams band a few times, thought it worse than Eureka and Young Tuxedo, which Bill Russell disagreed with.

segments.chapter: Bands and membership
segments.title: Massed bands at Booker T. Washington Auditorium and tuba duel
segments.summary: At Sunday school parades five bands played together on the steps, and two tuba players including Wilbert Tillman traded phrases.

segments.chapter: Bands and membership
segments.title: Band membership and continuity
segments.summary: Wood believed Eureka and Young Tuxedo had stable membership (Casimir, Jim Robinson, Tillman, Emil Knox), compared with Wratten's banner and shifting personnel today.

segments.chapter: French Quarter music, then and now
segments.title: Parties, passing the hat and tips
segments.summary: Wood never attended student parties with bands and saw no collections at parades, only tips at the Paddock Lounge.

segments.chapter: French Quarter music, then and now
segments.title: Decatur Street and the French Market in the 1950s
segments.summary: Wood never heard music on Decatur Street, recalling the fish market and Ruggiero's.

segments.chapter: French Quarter music, then and now
segments.title: Music in the French Quarter in recent summers
segments.summary: Wood describes the gazebo, Cafe Mediterranean and tent bands, Olympia Brass, the Junior Olympia band, and the Cafe Mediterranean group he finds too touristy.

segments.chapter: French Quarter music, then and now
segments.title: The French Market Jazz Band
segments.summary: Wood finds the French Market Jazz Band with Greg Stafford fine but falling short.

segments.chapter: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
segments.title: What Wood likes in traditional New Orleans music
segments.summary: Wood values restraint, melody and accessibility in traditional music and dislikes the Dukes of Dixieland as lacking depth.

segments.chapter: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
segments.title: The ragtime orchestra: is it jazz?
segments.summary: They discuss the New Orleans Ragtime Orchestra, reading versus improvising, and why Wood finds it a legitimate extension of the tradition.

segments.chapter: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
segments.title: Street cries and Creole speech
segments.summary: Wood recalls hardly any street cries and only a French-speaking family at Morrison's Cafeteria.

segments.chapter: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
segments.title: Eureka personnel; Paul Barbarin and Percy Humphrey
segments.summary: Wood remembers only Young Tuxedo's personnel; they sort out Barbarin's Onward Brass Band and Percy Humphrey as Eureka's leader.

segments.chapter: Traditional style, ragtime orchestra and closing questions
segments.title: Preservation Hall band visit to Bridgewater, Virginia
segments.summary: Wood begins a story of a Preservation Hall band booked at Bridgewater College on a cold February day in the late 1960s.
